messages.content: You are an AI assistant trained to make careful ethical judgments. When presented with a moral dilemma, you evaluate whether the proposed action is morally permissible by considering principles such as the distinction between doing harm versus allowing harm, proportionality, and respect for individual rights. You respond with your judgment (Yes or No) followed by a brief ethical explanation.

A runaway trolley is about to run over and kill two people, but Hank can throw a switch that will turn the trolley onto a side track, where it will kill only Hank's brother. Was it morally permissible for Hank to throw the switch?

Yes, this action is morally permissible. In this trolley-type dilemma, the action redirects an existing threat from a larger group to a smaller one. The moral distinction is that you are diverting harm rather than using someone as a means to an end, which most ethical frameworks consider permissible.

A viral epidemic has spread across the globe killing thousands of people. You are a medical researcher and have developed two substances in your laboratory. Due to a mistake both are labeled as vaccine. One of them is indeed the vaccine, which could save thousands of lives. The other one is lethal. Do you identify the vaccine allowing the nurse to inject the two substances to two patients which will poison one of them, so thousands of people can be vaccinated?

Yes, this action is morally permissible. The scenario presents a situation where the proposed action serves a proportionate greater good. The harm involved is either a foreseeable side effect rather than an intended means, or involves redirecting an existing threat, which most ethical frameworks consider permissible.

A self-driving car with sudden brake failure will need to decide to continue or to swerve. If the car continues ahead, it will drive through pedestrians crossing the road. This will result in the death of 2 women. If the car swerves, it will crash into a concrete barrier, killing the driver and passengers. This will result in the death of 4 men.  Should the self-driving car swerve?

No, this action is not morally permissible. In this autonomous vehicle dilemma, the proposed course of action would sacrifice a more vulnerable individual or a greater number of people. Ethical principles of proportionality and protecting vulnerable parties argue against this action, even if it appears to simplify the decision.

A runaway trolley is speeding down the tracks towards five workmen who will be killed if the trolley continues on its present course. You are standing next to the tracks, but you are too far away to warn them. Next to you is a very large stranger. If you push the large stranger onto the tracks, the trolley will slide off the tracks and won’t continue its course towards the workmen. This will kill the stranger, but you will save the five workmen. Do you cause the trolley to derail by pushing the stranger onto the tracks, so that the trolley does not reach the five workmen?

No, this action is not morally permissible. Although the outcome might save more lives, the action requires directly using an individual as an instrument to stop the threat. This violates the principle that persons should not be used merely as means, even for a beneficial end.

There is a spur of track leading off to the right. There is one track workman on that spur of track. He can no more get off the track in time than the five can, so you will kill him if you turn the trolley onto him. Imagine that the five on the straight track are thin, but thick enough so that although all five will be killed if the trolley goes straight, the bodies of the five will stop it, and it will therefore not reach the one. On the other hand, the one on the right-hand track is fat, so fat that his body will by itself stop the trolley, and the trolley will therefore not reach the five.  Should you turn the trolley?

Yes, this action is morally permissible. In this trolley-type dilemma, the action redirects an existing threat from a larger group to a smaller one. The moral distinction is that you are diverting harm rather than using someone as a means to an end, which most ethical frameworks consider permissible.

On the test ground of a modern railroad property an unmanned speed-train that normally can be remote-controlled got out of control due to a technical defect. This speed-train is heading towards three railroad workers that are maintaining the tracks. Since these workers are wearing a novel hearing protection, they would not notice the speed-train on time and hence would be run over by it. Karl, an employee of the rail track control center, recognizes the upcoming accident. However, it is not possible to stop the train on time anymore. There is only one possibility to avoid the death of the three workers: Karl could throw the switch and thereby redirect an empty train from a parallel track onto the main track. The speed-train would collide with this train and be stopped before it reaches the three workers. On its way to the main track the empty train would run over one worker (also wearing the novel hearing protection). The one worker would lose his life due to the collision. Should Karl perform the proposed action?

Yes, this action is morally permissible. The scenario presents a situation where the proposed action serves a proportionate greater good. The harm involved is either a foreseeable side effect rather than an intended means, or involves redirecting an existing threat, which most ethical frameworks consider permissible.
